\begin{theorem}

  \leanok
  \proven
  For any `k`, the three-cornered `(3k+2) × 2` rectangle is L-tileable.

  Split off a $3k\times 2$ full rectangle (left, tileable); right piece is $R^{-}(2,2)$.
  Example $k=2$: $8\times 2$ minus corner.
  \begin{center}\begin{tikzpicture}
    \drawgrid{8}{2}
    \foreach \x in {0,1,2,3,4,5}{\foreach \y in {0,1}{\filledcell{\x}{\y}{rectColor}}}
    \foreach \x in {6,7}{\filledcell{\x}{0}{minusColor}}
    \filledcell{6}{1}{minusColor}
    \removedcell{7}{1}
    \draw[dashed,thick,gray] ({6*\cs},0) -- ({6*\cs},{2*\cs});
    \node[above] at ({3*\cs},{2*\cs}) {\small rect $6\times 2$};
    \node[above] at ({6.5*\cs},{2*\cs}) {\small $R^{-}(2,2)$};
  \end{tikzpicture}\end{center}
\end{theorem}

  \label{tileable_5x_3kplus2_minus}

  \uses{tileable_5x_6kplus2_minus, tileable_5x_6kplus5_minus}
  \leanok
  \proven
  If `k` is odd or even, then `3k+2` is of the form `6k'+5` or `6k'+2` respectively,

  Split a $5\times 3k$ full rectangle off the bottom; top is $R^{-}(5,2)$ or $R^{-}(5,5)$.

  \begin{center}\begin{tikzpicture}

    \draw[dashed,thick,gray] (0,{6*\cs}) -- ({5*\cs},{6*\cs});

  \end{tikzpicture}\end{center}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{tileable_rectMinusCorner_mod2_jk_ge2}

  \uses{tileable_3kplus2_x2_minus, rect_tileable_iff}
  \leanok
  \proven
  For `j,k ≥ 2`, the three-cornered `(3j+2) × (3k+2)` rectangle is L-tileable.

  For $j,k\ge 2$: split a $(3j{+}2)\times 3k$ full rectangle off the bottom;
  top is $R^{-}(3j{+}2,2)$. Example $j=k=2$: $8\times 8$ minus corner.
  \begin{center}\begin{tikzpicture}
    \drawgrid{8}{8}
    \foreach \x in {0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7}{\foreach \y in {0,1,2,3,4,5}{\filledcell{\x}{\y}{rectColor}}}
    \foreach \x in {0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7}{\foreach \y in {6,7}{\filledcell{\x}{\y}{minusColor}}}
    \removedcell{7}{7}
    \draw[dashed,thick,gray] (0,{6*\cs}) -- ({8*\cs},{6*\cs});
    \node at ({4*\cs},{3*\cs}) {\small rect $(3j{+}2)\times 3k$};
    \node at ({4*\cs},{7*\cs}) {\small $R^{-}(8,2)$};
  \end{tikzpicture}\end{center}
\end{theorem}

\section{Helper lemmas for the mod 3 = 1 case}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{tileable_4x_rectMinus_3kplus1}
  \lean{tileable_4x_rectMinus_3kplus1}
  \uses{tileable_4x4_minus, rect_tileable_iff}
  \leanok
  \proven
  For `k ≥ 1`, the three-cornered `4 × (3k+1)` rectangle is L-tileable.

  Split a $4\times 3(k{-}1)$ full rectangle off the bottom; top is $R^{-}(4,4)$.
  Example $k=2$: $4\times 7$ minus corner.
  \begin{center}\begin{tikzpicture}
    \drawgrid{4}{7}
    \foreach \x in {0,1,2,3}{\foreach \y in {0,1,2}{\filledcell{\x}{\y}{rectColor}}}
    \foreach \x in {0,1,2,3}{\foreach \y in {3,4,5,6}{\filledcell{\x}{\y}{minusColor}}}
    \removedcell{3}{6}
    \draw[dashed,thick,gray] (0,{3*\cs}) -- ({4*\cs},{3*\cs});
    \node[right=2pt] at ({4*\cs},{1.5*\cs}) {\small rect $4\times 3$};
    \node[right=2pt] at ({4*\cs},{4.5*\cs}) {\small $R^{-}(4,4)$};
  \end{tikzpicture}\end{center}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{tileable_rect_mod1_by_mult3}
  \lean{tileable_rect_mod1_by_mult3}
  \leanok
  \proven
  Helper: If n = 3k + 1 with k ≥ 1, and j ≥ 3, then rectangle n (3(j-1)) is tileable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{tileable_rectMinusCorner_mod1_jk_ge}
  \lean{tileable_rectMinusCorner_mod1_jk_ge}
  \uses{tileable_4x_rectMinus_3kplus1, rect_tileable_iff}
  \leanok
  \proven
  If `n = 3k+1` and `m = 3j+1` with `j ≥ 3` and `k ≥ 1`, then

  For $n=3k{+}1$, $m=3j{+}1$, $j\ge 3$, $k\ge 1$: split a $(3k{+}1)\times 3(j{-}1)$
  full rectangle off the bottom; top is $R^{-}(3k{+}1,4)$.
  Example $j=3,k=1$: $4\times 10$ minus corner.
  \begin{center}\begin{tikzpicture}
    \drawgrid{4}{10}
    \foreach \x in {0,1,2,3}{\foreach \y in {0,1,2,3,4,5}{\filledcell{\x}{\y}{rectColor}}}
    \foreach \x in {0,1,2,3}{\foreach \y in {6,7,8,9}{\filledcell{\x}{\y}{minusColor}}}
    \removedcell{3}{9}
    \draw[dashed,thick,gray] (0,{6*\cs}) -- ({4*\cs},{6*\cs});
    \node[right=2pt] at ({4*\cs},{3*\cs}) {\small $(3k{+}1)\times 3(j{-}1)$};
    \node[right=2pt] at ({4*\cs},{7.5*\cs}) {\small $R^{-}(4,4)$};
  \end{tikzpicture}\end{center}
\end{theorem}

  \begin{center}\begin{tikzpicture}

      (0,{6*\cs}) -- (\cs,{6*\cs}) -- (\cs,{7*\cs}) -- (0,{7*\cs}) -- cycle;
    \draw[blue!70!black,ultra thick]
      (0,{7*\cs}) -- ({2*\cs},{7*\cs}) -- ({2*\cs},{8*\cs}) -- (0,{8*\cs}) -- cycle;

    \draw[orange!80!black,ultra thick] (\cs,{6*\cs}) rectangle ({4*\cs},{7*\cs});
    \node[left=2pt] at (0,{3*\cs}) {\tiny piece2: rot.\ $R^{-}(4,7)$};
    \node[left=2pt] at (0,{7.5*\cs}) {\tiny piece1: tromino};
  \end{tikzpicture}\end{center}
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{tileable_rectangleMinus2Corner_3jplus1_3kplus2}
  \lean{tileable_rectangleMinus2Corner_3jplus1_3kplus2}
  \uses{tileable_rectangleMinus2Corner_4_3kplus2, tileable_rectangleMinus2Corner_3jplus2_3kplus1}
  \leanok
  \proven
  \((tileable\_rectangleMinus2Corner\_3jplus1\_3kplus2)\)

  Three sub-cases for $R^{--}(3j{+}1,3k{+}2)$:

  \smallskip\noindent\textbf{(a) $j\ge 3$:} left strip $3(j{-}1)\times(3k{+}2)$ + right $R^{--}(4,3k{+}2)$.
  Example $j=3,k=1$: $R^{--}(10,5)$.
  \begin{center}\begin{tikzpicture}
    \drawgrid{10}{5}
    \foreach \x in {0,1,2,3,4,5}{\foreach \y in {0,1,2,3,4}{\filledcell{\x}{\y}{yellow!70}}}
    \foreach \x in {6,7,8,9}{\foreach \y in {0,1,2,3,4}{\filledcell{\x}{\y}{minusColor}}}
    \removedcell{8}{4}\removedcell{9}{4}
    \draw[dashed,thick,gray] ({6*\cs},0) -- ({6*\cs},{5*\cs});
    \node at ({3*\cs},{2.5*\cs}) {\small $3(j{-}1)\times(3k{+}2)$};
    \node at ({8*\cs},{2*\cs}) {\small $R^{--}(4,5)$};
  \end{tikzpicture}\end{center}

  \smallskip\noindent\textbf{(b) $j=2$, $k$ even:} left strip $3\times(3k{+}2)$ + right $R^{--}(4,3k{+}2)$.
  Example $j=2,k=2$: $R^{--}(7,8)$.
  \begin{center}\begin{tikzpicture}
    \drawgrid{7}{8}
    \foreach \x in {0,1,2}{\foreach \y in {0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7}{\filledcell{\x}{\y}{yellow!70}}}
    \foreach \x in {3,4,5,6}{\foreach \y in {0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7}{\filledcell{\x}{\y}{minusColor}}}
    \removedcell{5}{7}\removedcell{6}{7}
    \draw[dashed,thick,gray] ({3*\cs},0) -- ({3*\cs},{8*\cs});
    \node at ({1.5*\cs},{4*\cs}) {\small $3\times(3k{+}2)$};
    \node at ({5*\cs},{3.5*\cs}) {\small $R^{--}(4,8)$};
  \end{tikzpicture}\end{center}

  \smallskip\noindent\textbf{(c) $j=2$, $k$ odd:} pieces A ($\cong R^{--}(5,4)$), B (L-tromino), C ($3\times4$ rect).
  Example $j=2,k=1$: $R^{--}(7,5)$.
  \begin{center}\begin{tikzpicture}
    \drawgrid{7}{5}
    \foreach \x in {0,1,2,3}{\foreach \y in {0,1,2}{\filledcell{\x}{\y}{pieceAcolor}}}
    \foreach \x in {0,1,2}{\filledcell{\x}{3}{pieceAcolor}\filledcell{\x}{4}{pieceAcolor}}
    \filledcell{3}{3}{pieceBcolor}\filledcell{3}{4}{pieceBcolor}\filledcell{4}{4}{pieceBcolor}
    \foreach \x in {4,5,6}{\foreach \y in {0,1,2,3}{\filledcell{\x}{\y}{pieceCcolor}}}
    \removedcell{5}{4}\removedcell{6}{4}
    \draw[green!50!black,ultra thick] (0,0) rectangle ({4*\cs},{3*\cs});
    \draw[green!50!black,ultra thick] (0,{3*\cs}) rectangle ({3*\cs},{5*\cs});
    \draw[red!60!black,ultra thick]
      ({3*\cs},{3*\cs}) -- ({4*\cs},{3*\cs}) -- ({4*\cs},{4*\cs}) -- ({5*\cs},{4*\cs})
      -- ({5*\cs},{5*\cs}) -- ({3*\cs},{5*\cs}) -- cycle;
    \draw[purple!60!black,ultra thick] ({4*\cs},0) rectangle ({7*\cs},{4*\cs});
    \node at ({1.5*\cs},{1.5*\cs}) {\small A};
    \node at ({3.7*\cs},{4.2*\cs}) {\small B};
    \node at ({5.5*\cs},{2*\cs}) {\small C};
  \end{tikzpicture}\end{center}
\end{theorem}

  A tileset is valid for a region if tiles are disjoint and exactly cover it
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
  \label{instDecidablePairwiseDisjoint}
  \lean{instDecidablePairwiseDisjoint}
  \leanok
  \proven
  Decidable pairwise disjointness for finite index types
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
  \label{instDecidableValid}
  \lean{instDecidableValid}
  \leanok
  \proven
  Decidable validity for finite index types
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{Valid_disjoint_tiles}
  \lean{Valid.disjoint_tiles}
  \leanok
  \proven
  Tiles at different indices are disjoint
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{Valid_tile_contained}
  \lean{Valid.tile_contained}
  \leanok
  \proven
  Every tile's cells are contained in the region
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}
  \label{translate}
  \lean{translate}
  \leanok
  \proven
  Translate a tileset by an offset

\begin{theorem}
  \label{translate_preserves_disjoint}
  \lean{translate_preserves_disjoint}

  Translation of a tileset translates coverage

\begin{theorem}
  \label{translate_preserves_valid}

\section{General Tileability}

\begin{definition}
  \label{Tileable}
  \lean{Tileable}
  \leanok
  \proven
  A region is tileable by a protoset if there exists a valid tiling
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{empty_tileable}
  \lean{empty_tileable}
  \leanok
  \proven
  The empty region is tileable by any protoset
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{Tileable_translate}
  \lean{Tileable_translate}
  \leanok
  \proven
  A translated tileable region is tileable by any protoset
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{Tileable_union}
  \lean{Tileable_union}
  \leanok
  \proven
  If two disjoint regions are both tileable, their union is tileable
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{Tileable_biUnion}
  \lean{Tileable_biUnion}
  \leanok
  \proven
  Finite union of pairwise-disjoint tileable regions is tileable.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{translateRegion_neg}
  \lean{translateRegion_neg}
  \leanok
  \proven
  Translating by offset and then by `-offset` gives the original region
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{translateRegion_add}
  \lean{translateRegion_add}
  \leanok
  \proven
  Composition of translations on a region adds their offsets.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{erase_union_finset}
  \lean{erase_union_finset}
  \leanok
  \proven
  Erasing a point from a finite union distributes over both sides.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{translateRegion_erase_point}
  \lean{translateRegion_erase_point}
  \leanok
  \proven
  Erasing a translated point is the same as translating an erased region.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{Tileable_translate_iff}
  \lean{Tileable_translate_iff}
  \leanok
  \proven
  Tileability is preserved by translation (both directions)
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{Tileable_of_translate_eq}
  \lean{Tileable_of_translate_eq}
  \leanok
  \proven
  If `R = translateRegion S offset` and `R` is tileable, then `S` is tileable
\end{theorem}

\begin{definition}
  \label{PlacedTile_containedIn}
  \lean{PlacedTile.containedIn}
  \leanok

  A placed tile is contained in a region if all its cells are in the region

\begin{definition}
  \label{PlacedTile_coversCell}
  \lean{PlacedTile.coversCell}
  \leanok
  \proven
  A placed tile covers a cell if the cell is in its cells
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
  \label{allPlacementsCoveringProto}
  \lean{allPlacementsCoveringProto}
  \leanok
  \proven
  All placements of a single prototile that cover a given target cell.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}
  \label{allPlacementsCovering}
  \lean{allPlacementsCovering}
  \leanok
  \proven
  All placements from a protoset that cover a given target cell
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{allPlacementsCoveringProto_covers}
  \lean{allPlacementsCoveringProto_covers}
  \leanok

  \label{allPlacementsCoveringProto_complete}
  \lean{allPlacementsCoveringProto_complete}

\begin{definition}

  \leanok

\section{Protoset Refinement}

\begin{definition}
  \label{Refines}
  \lean{Refines}
  \leanok
  \proven
  `psA` refines `psB` if every rotated prototile of `psB` is tileable by `psA`.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{Tileable_refine}
  \lean{Tileable_refine}
  \leanok
  \proven
  If `psA` refines `psB` and `psB` tiles `R`, then `psA` tiles `R`.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}

\begin{theorem}
  \label{rectangle_split_vertical}
  \lean{rectangle_split_vertical}
